scenes.heading: BigQuery Partitioning & Clustering
scenes.narration: Partitioning and clustering are the two levers that cut how much data BigQuery scans, saving both time and money.

scenes.heading: Partitioning vs clustering

left.title: Partitioning
points: Usually by date or ingestion time

scenes.narration: Partitioning divides a table into coarse segments, most often by date, so a query can skip entire partitions. Clustering sorts the rows inside each partition by chosen columns to enable finer block pruning. Used together they narrow scans from the partition level down to the block level.

scenes.heading: Why it matters for cost
bullets: On-demand pricing bills by bytes scanned, so pruning directly cuts cost.
A date filter on a partitioned table can skip years of data instantly.
Clustering helps most on high-cardinality filter and join columns.
Require partition filters to stop expensive accidental full scans.
scenes.narration: Because you pay for the bytes a query reads, pruning is the most direct way to lower cost. A well-placed date filter on a partitioned table can skip almost all the data. Adding clustering on the columns you filter and join on prunes even further within each partition.

scenes.heading: Creating a partitioned, clustered table
scenes.code:
CREATE TABLE sales.events
  PARTITION BY DATE(event_ts)
  CLUSTER BY country, product_id
AS SELECT * FROM sales.raw_events;

-- This query prunes to one day, one country
SELECT product_id, COUNT(*)
FROM sales.events
WHERE DATE(event_ts) = '2026-07-01'
  AND country = 'US'
GROUP BY product_id;
scenes.narration: The table is partitioned by the event date and clustered by country and product, which organizes the data for pruning. The query then filters on a single day and a single country. BigQuery reads only that one partition and the matching clustered blocks, so it scans a tiny fraction of the table.

scenes.text: Partition on your date filter and cluster on your common filter columns to scan less and pay less.
scenes.narration: Partition by the column you always filter on and cluster by the rest, and every query will scan far less data.
